messages.subject: Re: strata/bootstrapping question
parts:
Tina-

It is impossible to offer good advice without knowing some information
about your sampling situation (how many transects, how were they chosen
etc) and why you want to get abundance by transect and what you are
going to do with it. If you want density by transect(sample) you can
simply click on that as well as a global estimate to get it as well. If
you think that detection varies by transect, I'd evaluate that as a
covariate using MCDS. From what I can tell, you don't need to use
post-stratification.

--jeff

On 3/15/2010 1:34 AM, C. Blewett wrote:
> > Hello list.
> >
> > I searched archives and did not find an answer to this question.
> >
> > I have replicate transects and want to estimate density for each transect. I also want a "global" density estimate. My # of observations for each transect range from 26 to 107 observations.
> >
> > Question #1) Should I simply post-stratify by sample (transect) and select detection, encounter
> > rate and density to be calculated for strata level, and also then a global
> > density? There was something in the manual that said for post-stratifying have> 15 observations for a reliable estimate of the detection function per strata. but that seems still a bit small.... and 28 is fairly close to that.
> >
> > or Question #2 ) Would it be better to select to calculate the detection function at the Global level and then calculate density at both the Strata and Global level? (Then if yes, according to the Distance manual, if I do this, I HAVE to calculate confidence intervals for the global estimate with bootstrapping, so would this be bootstrapping at the sample level, or bootstrapping at the observation level?)
> >
> > or Question 3) Would I gain much precision by bootstrapping observations to the sample level to get a better estimate of each strata (the samples/transects)? Or do you think that 28-107 observations per transect is sufficient for calculating a detection function?
> >
> > Thanks!
> > Tina Blewett

messages.author: 5140016d70f6ba82
messages.subject: Re: strata/bootstrapping question
parts:
Below is what Tina sent me off-list. The following is my advice. I'm
sending to the list as well in hopes that others might chime in. I think
this exchange demonstrates the importance of providing all of the
details about the study objective and design when you ask questions on
this list that request analysis advice rather than how-to questions
about DISTANCE. The latter requires far less details than the former.

From what I gather your main focus is to relate bird density to other
biological aspects and NOT to infer total abundance in a region. As
such, your primary focus is to estimate density on each transect in each
season. That's fine but it suggests a much different approach than
suggested by your initial query. Given your description, I would create
12 strata (2 seasons * 6 transects) and within each strata I would
define a sample for each visit to that transect. Then I would use MCDS
and I would investigate whether rainy/dry, transect, species and other
variables(?) might affect detection probability. If you are
uncomfortable using transect, I'd at least consider using habitat or
some other variable that might differ by transect that could affect
detection probability. If you reject this outright, you risk
confounding or adding noise to your analysis across transects with
detection variation. You can fit additive models which require far
fewer parameters than fitting a separate detection function for each
species on each transect.

Then I'd estimate density by strata and if you want to bootstrap, you
can bootstrap samples within stratum which is using your replicate
visits to asses variation in density on each transect. Personally, I
don't think you'll gain much from the bootstrap but you can certainly
try it.

Estimating average density across strata will be easy because if you
assign area=1 for each strata then you'll get the average density.
However, doing so within the rainy/dry season would be more difficult
but could be done by outside of Distance. Alternatively, you could
split the analysis and do dry/rainy separately by selecting and
analyzing each set of strata separately.

The one gotcha in all of this is that your transect estimates will be
correlated unless you estimate detection separately for each species on
each transect. That will complicate your later analysis and I suggest
that you may want to look at a recent paper that Steve Buckland wrote on
this subject. Can't remember the citation at present but maybe Steve
can chime in. regards --jeff

On 3/16/2010 12:04 PM, C. Blewett wrote:
> > I don't know how much information and detail you want about the
> > project. it was on an island, in tropical rain forest, for 3 species
> > of birds. But I can only use Distance on 2 of the species.
> > Basically I want a density from Distance for each bird species per
> > each transect per season, and then global density (pooled across
> > season: dry and rainy). You asked what I'm using it for - I'm using
> > these data as one of the descriptions of data we collected at each
> > transect (more below). After thinking about it, I really don't think
> > it would be wise to model probability of detection for each transect
> > separately, I feel it's best to be conservative and use the global
> > probability of detection (all transects pooled per season).
> > If you're interested, we had 6 transects, and repeated the surveys
> > over 2 seasons. We visited each transect 13 times total for 78 total
> > transect visits. 7 visits per each of 6 transects in the dry season
> > and 6 visits per each of 6 transects in the rainy. So all visits to
> > each transect are pooled (per season) as if each were one long
> > transect. I am estimating density separately (using separate models,
> > etc) for rainy and dry seasons.
> > So for an estimate per transect, it lists in the manual on P110 this
> > scenario exactly where post-stratification may be useful. But I will
> > compare those results to just "checking" the density box under Sample
> > like you mentioned. I did notice that it changes the encounter rate
> > parameter from global to sample. It does not seem to change the
> > density estimate, but it changed the variance.
> > Info on my sites: the 6 transects are 1 km long each, chosen by
> > stratification because of elevation. Sorry, not purely randomized, I
> > know I know. :) So for these data I am just inferring density over
> > area sampled (setting under the variance tab to use the Poisson with
> > overdispersion to 0, etc.). I can give more information on the site
> > selection process if you want it.
> > More info on what I am doing with bird densities: The density of the
> > bird species per site is just one metric we collected. We have per
> > site behavioral observations (foraging, nesting, singing, etc),
> > seasonality, nesting phenology, we found nests, recorded calls, netted
> > birds for morphometrics and to collect DNA samples, took vegetation
> > measurements along the transect. Do you think that this is an invalid
> > use of a bird density estimate? We necessarily had to have fewer
> > sites because we wanted to visit each site many times, and do so much
> > per site.
> > Did I not read that bootstrapping gives a more robust estimate of
> > variance when sample sie is small? I thought bootstrapping might be
> > recomended in this case because we only have 6 transects. Would that
> > give a better (less biased) measure of variance? running the density
> > analysis for the data pooled for an entire season, bootstrapping the
> > samples for the global density estimate?
> > Any other advice you can offer is greatly appreciated. Thank you!
> > Tina Blewett
